keywords: how are loafers supposed to fit
answer: Loafers should fit snugly from the start: your toes about ¼–⅜ in from the end, firm but comfortable pressure across the instep, and your heel lifting no more than about ¼ in as you walk. With no laces to tighten, a loafer that feels roomy in the store will feel loose once the leather softens.
intro: A loafer holds your foot only by its shape: the vamp over the instep and the heel counter behind. Leather loafers also stretch and mold more than laced shoes. So the rule is to buy them a little snugger than a lace-up, but never short in length, because leather gives in width, not in length.

checklist.good: The vamp, the leather over the top of your foot, presses evenly and firmly without pinching. You can't easily slide a finger under it.
checklist.tooTight: The vamp presses painfully on the top of your foot, or leaves a red mark after a few minutes.
checklist.tooLoose: The vamp sits away from your foot or gapes at the sides, and the shoe slides around when you walk.

checklist.good: Your heel sits in the counter and lifts slightly, up to about ¼ in, in new stiff-soled loafers. That lift reduces as the sole flexes.
checklist.tooTight: The back edge cuts into your heel or Achilles tendon.
checklist.tooLoose: Your heel pops out with each step, or you can slip a finger behind it while standing.

checklist.good: About ¼–⅜ in between your longest toe and the end of the shoe, a little closer than in a sneaker.
checklist.tooTight: Too short: your toes touch the end or curl. Leather won't stretch this away.
checklist.tooLoose: Too long: more than ½ in of space, a deep crease behind the toe, and your heel slipping.

checklist.good: Snug across the ball of the foot, with light pressure that eases over the first few wears.
checklist.tooTight: Sharp pressure on the big-toe or little-toe joint, or the leather bulges over the welt.
checklist.tooLoose: Your foot slides side to side and the leather wrinkles across the forefoot.

checklist.good: The edge of the opening sits flat against your foot all round, including below the ankle bones.
checklist.tooTight: The topline digs into the sides of your foot or your ankle bones.
checklist.tooLoose: The sides gape open when you walk or flex your foot.

variations.heading: Fit by loafer style
variations.intro: Construction and lining change how much a loafer gives.

items.name: Penny and dress loafers
items.text: Stiffer leather and a firm sole mean some heel lift at first. Fit them snug across the instep; the leather will relax a little but the length won't change.

items.name: Unlined and suede loafers
items.text: These stretch the most. They should feel close-fitting, almost tight across the vamp, when new. Many people go a half size down in unlined suede compared with their lace-up size.

items.name: Driving moccasins
items.text: Soft and flexible, with rubber pebbles on the sole. They should fit like a glove with no heel slip, because they mold quickly and have little structure to hold the foot.

items.name: Horsebit and tassel loafers
items.text: The same rules apply. Hardware and tassels don't change the fit, but a lower-cut vamp gives less hold, so check heel slip carefully.

items.name: Men's and women's loafers
items.text: The checkpoints are the same. Women's loafers are often cut lower at the vamp, which gives less grip over the instep, so the heel fit matters even more.

measure.heading: How to choose your loafer size
steps: Start from your dress-shoe size, measured late in the day, not your sneaker size.
Try the loafers with the socks you'll wear: thin dress socks, no-show socks or bare feet.
Stand and press the toe to confirm about ¼–⅜ in of space.
Walk on a hard floor and check heel slip in a mirror from behind.
If you're between two sizes and both are the right length, choose the snugger one. If the smaller is short in length, take the larger and add a tongue pad.
measure.tip: If you'll wear loafers sockless, try them on barefoot. A sock can take up nearly a half size in a slip-on.

problems.fix: Some lift is normal when new. If it's more than about ¼ in, add a heel grip inside the counter or an adhesive tongue pad under the vamp, which pushes your heel back into the cup.

problems.problem: Loafers stretched and now feel loose
problems.fix: A tongue pad or a thin full-length insole takes up the extra volume. Next pair, buy a half size snugger.

problems.problem: Vamp presses on the top of the foot
problems.fix: A cobbler can stretch the vamp with a stretcher. If you have a high instep, look for loafers with a higher vamp or a split vamp.
The loafer is too wide or too big. A narrower width or a half size down fits better; a tongue pad helps a little.

extra.heading: Breaking in loafers
extra.body: Wear new leather loafers around the house for an hour or two at a time over a week. The leather softens over the instep and the sole starts to flex, which cuts heel slip. A blister plaster on the back of the heel helps in the first few wears. If they still hurt after a week or two, they likely won't improve.

extra.heading: Wearing loafers without socks
extra.body: No-show socks keep sweat off the leather and reduce rubbing while looking sockless. If you do go bare, try the loafers on barefoot, dust the inside with foot powder, and give them a day off between wears to dry out.

picks.label: Leather loafers in half sizes and widths
picks.why: Loafers depend on a close fit, so half sizes and width options make it easier to get one.

picks.label: Adhesive tongue pads
picks.why: Push your foot back into the heel and take up space in loafers that have loosened.

picks.label: No-show socks with heel grips
picks.why: Stay hidden in loafers and have a silicone heel to stop the sock from slipping down.
picks.query: no show socks silicone heel grip

faqs.q: Should loafers be tight or loose?
faqs.a: Snug. Loafers should feel close across the instep and at the heel when new, because leather loafers loosen with wear and there are no laces to tighten.

faqs.q: Should loafers slip at the heel?
faqs.a: A little lift, up to about ¼ inch, is normal in new loafers with stiff soles and fades as the sole breaks in. If your heel comes out of the shoe, they're too big.

faqs.q: Should you size down in loafers?
faqs.a: Many people go a half size down from their sneaker size, especially in unlined or suede loafers. Never size down so far that your toes touch the end.
The same as any loafer: about ¼–⅜ inch at the toe, firm pressure across the instep, and minimal heel slip. Size from your dress-shoe size rather than your sneaker size.
Yes. Leather and suede loafers stretch in width and across the vamp, often noticeably. They don't get longer.

faqs.q: How much room should be in the toe of a loafer?
faqs.a: About ¼–⅜ inch, roughly the width of your little finger, between your longest toe and the end.
